title: High Impact Teaching Strategies as sustained science practice
subtitle: Ten evidence-based instructional practices, each worked through as a term-length arc in a real NSW science context — Stage 4 and 5 focus areas from the Science 7–10 Syllabus (2023), and Stage 6 modules from the current science syllabuses.
kicker: NSW secondary science · a resource for beginning teachers and mentors
thesis: A HITS is not a lesson activity. Read the Victorian department's own exemplars closely and none of them is a single moment: they run across terms, are planned in teams, are monitored with data, and are evaluated and revised. The unit of implementation is a term, not a lesson. Every exemplar here is built that way.
usageNote:
Pick a strategy, then read the arc. Each exemplar opens with a real problem of practice, then runs as four or five phases across a term. The coloured bar is a week ruler — click a segment to jump to that phase. Underneath sit the teacher and student indicators, a four-level continuum of practice written for science, and what the teacher used to judge whether it worked.

Read the phases, not just the headline. The interesting part of most of these arcs is phase 3 or 4 — the point where the scaffold is deliberately faded, or where the data comes back and the plan changes. That is where the strategy stops being a technique and becomes practice.

On jurisdictions. The HITS framework is a Victorian Department of Education resource, and the effect sizes quoted are Hattie's, as reported in that document. The syllabus contexts here are all NSW. The NSW equivalent framework is CESE's What Works Best (2020 update; a 2025 edition is now published), built on eight themes — high expectations, explicit teaching, effective feedback, use of data to inform practice, assessment, classroom management, wellbeing and collaboration. The overlap is substantial but not one-to-one, and the two use different organising logic. If you're programming in a NSW public school, What Works Best is the framework your school improvement documents will speak; HITS is a useful second lens, particularly for its granularity about worked examples, multiple exposures and lesson structure.

A caution the HITS document makes itself. These strategies are described as reliable, not infallible. An effect size is an average across many studies and contexts; it is not a promise about your Year 9 class on a Friday afternoon. Each arc below therefore ends with how the teacher checked, because that is the part that makes the strategy answerable to your own students.
